analysis.one_liner: Caps company stock in workers' 401(k) accounts at 20% and lets workers sell company match shares.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was written after corporate collapses like Enron showed workers losing retirement savings that were concentrated in their own employer's stock. It would have barred 401(k)-type plans from letting any worker's account hold more than 20% in company stock and real property, and given workers the right to sell company shares their employer deposited as a match and reinvest elsewhere, starting 90 days after the deposit. It also shortened the wait before employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) participants can diversify from 10 years to 5 years and age 55 to 35, and cut in half the tax deduction employers get for matching worker contributions with their own stock.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with 401(k)-style accounts, especially at companies that match contributions in their own stock. The 20% cap would have prevented employers from loading an employee's retirement account with company shares, and the divestment right would have let workers sell those shares within 90 days instead of being locked in during blackout periods — the situation that cost Enron employees their savings.

how_it_helps.text: Caps employer stock and real property at 20% of any worker's individual account balance, so a single employer's collapsing share price could no longer wipe out most of a retirement account.
Lets workers direct the plan to sell employer stock or property from their account and reinvest the same amount in other assets, at any time starting 90 days after the shares are allocated to them.

Lets ESOP participants diversify out of employer stock after 5 years of service and at age 35, down from the prior 10-year and age-55 waits, with younger participants' distributions moved directly into another retirement plan.
Cuts the tax deduction for employer matching contributions made in company stock by half, reducing the tax incentive for employers to fill worker accounts with their own shares.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that match worker 401(k) contributions with their own stock would lose half the tax deduction for those matches and would have to keep employee holdings under the 20% cap. Companies with large stock matches might shift matches to cash or reduce them, and some workers who voluntarily want heavy company-stock exposure would lose that option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that match in their own stock

drawbacks.text: Halving the tax deduction for stock-match contributions could cause some employers to reduce or end their matching contributions, meaning some workers could get a smaller match even though the match itself was the problem only when paid in stock.

The 20% cap applies to all workers regardless of choice, so employees who deliberately want to hold more company stock — for example at a fast-growing employer — could not; the bill responds to Enron-style risk by removing individual discretion rather than only protecting against forced holdings.
The bill exempts ESOPs from the 20% cap entirely, so the plans with the heaviest single-stock concentration keep their old rules and get only the new 5-year/age-35 diversification rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers whose accounts are filled with employer stock, the protections are substantial and the mechanism is targeted: a cap plus a sell-back right addresses exactly the loss pattern the corporate collapses exposed. The main costs fall on employers using stock matches, and there is a real chance some would trim matches rather than pay in cash; forcing diversification on workers who would choose concentration is a genuine trade-off. On balance the bill offered workers meaningful protection at a modest cost to a specific employer practice.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees in January 2002 and later to a Ways and Means subcommittee, which never acted; no hearing, mark-up, or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Pascrell introduced the bill on January 29, 2002, during the wave of congressional concern over workers losing retirement savings concentrated in employer stock after corporate collapses.
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, splitting jurisdiction over its pension and tax provisions.
On May 9, 2002, part of the bill was referred to the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill attracted only three cosponsors, all House Democrats, and never advanced to a hearing, mark-up, or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that match worker retirement contributions with their own stock are better off: they kept the full tax deduction for stock matches and faced no cap on how much company stock ends up in employee accounts. Plan sponsors avoided the compliance changes, and workers at those companies remain exposed to concentrated employer stock unless their own plan offers diversification.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers matching 401(k)s in their own stock

industries.industry: Employers that match 401(k) contributions in their own stock
industries.note: The bill halves their tax deduction for stock matches and caps how much company stock can sit in employee accounts, removing a way to shore up their own share price with worker savings. Workers at these companies were the people the cap was written to protect.

ESOPs are exempt from the 20% cap, preserving the single-stock concentration that defines them, but their participants gain diversification rights after 5 years of service and at age 35, with younger participants' distributions moved directly into other retirement plans.

New quarterly 20% compliance tests, divestment mechanics, and diversification rules would have created ongoing administration work, but also a market for services helping workers rebalance out of employer stock.
